Amazeballs
uh-MAYZ-bawlz
adjective (Millennial slang)
A jokey intensification of amazing, formed by clipping to amaze and adding the nonsense suffix -balls (as in cuteballs). It appears online about 2008, was popularized by celebrity bloggers including Perez Hilton, and was famously added to the online Collins English Dictionary in 2012 after a public vote, prompting a round of complaints about the decline of English. By the mid-2010s it was used chiefly ironically.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Amazeballs means "amazing," said with a wink: a word that knows it is a little ridiculous. It belongs to the Millennial habit of playful inflation, where everything good is "amazing" and the extra suffix makes the word funny again. The Christian observation: there is nothing sinful in a silly word, and Christians are allowed to be playful. But the habit behind it, inflating ordinary things into wonders, has a cost, and the root word deserves a second look. In Webster’s 1828, to amaze was "To confound with fear, sudden surprise, or wonder." That is the word the Gospels use for real encounters with God. When Jesus healed the paralytic, "they were all amazed, and glorified God, saying, We never saw it on this fashion" (Mar 2:12). After the resurrection the women fled the tomb, "for they trembled and were amazed" (Mar 16:8). True amazement is the right response to the works of God, and it is not cheap. A people who spend "amazing" on lip gloss may have nothing left when they stand before the empty tomb. "Marvellous are thy works; and that my soul knoweth right well" (Psa 139:14). A father can laugh at amazeballs with his teenager, and then take him outside on a clear night, or to the bedside of a newborn, and let him feel what amazement actually is.

Webster 1828 Definition

Millennial jokey slang (c. 2008; Collins online 2012) for amazing; harmless play, though its root, amaze, names the trembling wonder the Gospels reserve for the works of God (Mar 16:8).

AMAZEBALLS, adj. (Millennial slang, c. 2008–2010s; from amaze + jocular -balls) Amazing; excellent; usually said ironically. "Your cupcakes are amazeballs."

Webster (1828), root amaze: AMAZE, verb transitive To confound with fear, sudden surprise, or wonder; to astonish. They shall be afraid; they shall be amazed at one another. Isaiah 23:1 . They were all amazed and glorified God. Mark 2:12 . Luke 5:26 . This word implies astonishment or perplexity, arising from something extraordinary, unexpected, unaccountable, or frightful.

Decode for parents: harmless; a chance to show children what real amazement feels like.

Key Scripture

Mar 2:12 — "And immediately he arose, took up the bed, and went forth before them all; insomuch that they were all amazed, and glorified God, saying, We never saw it on this fashion."

Mar 16:8 — "And they went out quickly, and fled from the sepulchre; for they trembled and were amazed: neither said they any thing to any man; for they were afraid."

Psa 139:14 — "I will praise thee; for I am fearfully and wonderfully made: marvellous are thy works; and that my soul knoweth right well."

Psa 8:1 — "O LORD our Lord, how excellent is thy name in all the earth! who hast set thy glory above the heavens."

Luk 5:26 — "And they were all amazed, and they glorified God, and were filled with fear, saying, We have seen strange things to day."

Modern Corruption

Amazeballs is playful inflation; its only lesson is the cheapening of amazement, which Scripture keeps for the works of God that make men tremble.

expand to see more

The quiet drift is that wonder becomes a tone of voice rather than a response to reality. When everything is amazing, nothing amazes, and the young lose the experience of being stopped in their tracks. The crowds who saw Jesus heal "were all amazed, and they glorified God, and were filled with fear, saying, We have seen strange things to day" (Luk 5:26). Amazement in Scripture is never a casual adjective; it is a man undone by glory.

The recovery is not to ban silly words but to cultivate real wonder. "O LORD our Lord, how excellent is thy name in all the earth!" (Psa 8:1). Read the young the miracles slowly, show them the stars, let them hold a newborn, and talk about what it means. Then their "amazeballs" at a dessert will stay a joke, and their amazement before God will be the real thing.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old English amasian (to stupefy) → amaze (to confound with fear or wonder) → amazing → c. 2008 amazeballs → Collins online 2012.
